clinicalPearls: SPG13 is a rare autosomal dominant, usually pure (uncomplicated) hereditary spastic paraplegia caused by heterozygous mutations in HSPD1, the gene encoding the mitochondrial chaperonin HSP60.
It presents in adulthood with slowly progressive lower-limb spasticity, hyperreflexia, extensor plantar responses and a spastic gait, while the upper limbs and bulbar function are typically spared.
Spasticity generally exceeds weakness, and although mild reduction of distal vibration sense can occur, prominent sensory, cerebellar or cognitive involvement argues against SPG13.
Bladder urgency may develop as corticospinal tract degeneration advances.

HSP60 works with its co-chaperonin HSP10 to fold nuclear-encoded proteins imported into the mitochondrial matrix, so SPG13 is fundamentally a disorder of mitochondrial protein folding affecting the long corticospinal axons.
Recessive (biallelic) HSPD1 mutations cause an entirely different, severe infantile hypomyelinating leukodystrophy, so zygosity and phenotype must always be interpreted together.
Diagnosis is clinical together with HSPD1 testing within a hereditary spastic paraplegia gene panel, after structural and acquired myelopathies have been excluded.
reference.pathophysiology: SPG13 is caused by heterozygous, typically missense, mutations in HSPD1 on chromosome 2q33, which encodes heat-shock protein 60 (HSP60), a mitochondrial matrix chaperonin. HSP60 assembles into a double-ring complex and, with its co-chaperonin HSP10, forms an enclosed chamber in which nuclear-encoded proteins imported into the mitochondrion fold correctly through an energy-dependent cycle. Disease-causing mutations reduce chaperonin folding capacity, compromising mitochondrial proteostasis and energy metabolism; because the longest corticospinal axons are the most metabolically vulnerable, the result is a length-dependent distal axonopathy that produces progressive lower-limb spasticity. Dominant SPG13 reflects a partial loss-of-function or dominant-negative mechanism, whereas complete biallelic loss of HSP60 function produces the severe recessive hypomyelinating leukodystrophy phenotype.
additionalDifferentials: SPG4 (SPAST) — the commonest autosomal dominant pure hereditary spastic paraplegia and the key differential
SPG3A (ATL1) — early-onset dominant pure hereditary spastic paraplegia
SPG31 (REEP1) and SPG6 (NIPA1) — other dominant pure hereditary spastic paraplegias
SPG7 (paraplegin) — a mitochondrial hereditary spastic paraplegia, usually recessive and often complicated
Primary lateral sclerosis and other motor-neuron disorders
Structural or compressive myelopathy, dopa-responsive dystonia and treatable myelopathies (vitamin B12 or copper deficiency, HTLV-1) as mimics
additionalInvestigations: HSPD1 analysis within a hereditary spastic paraplegia gene panel or exome
Exclusion of SPG4/SPAST and the other common hereditary spastic paraplegia genes
MRI of the brain and whole spine to exclude compressive, structural and demyelinating causes
Screen for treatable myelopathies, including vitamin B12, copper, very-long-chain fatty acids and HTLV-1 serology
Nerve conduction studies and electromyography to characterise any peripheral involvement and exclude motor-neuron disease
Family pedigree analysis and genetic counselling with cascade testing
redFlags: A sensory level, back pain or acute sphincter loss suggests a compressive or structural myelopathy that needs urgent imaging.
Bulbar symptoms, marked wasting or widespread fasciculations point towards motor-neuron disease.
Prominent cognitive decline, cerebellar signs or a significant peripheral neuropathy suggest a complicated hereditary spastic paraplegia or an alternative diagnosis.
Infantile onset with developmental regression indicates the recessive HSPD1 leukodystrophy rather than SPG13.
reference.prognosis: SPG13 is slowly progressive over years to decades with a normal life expectancy; many patients remain ambulant, although walking aids may eventually be required.
pitfalls: Confusing dominant SPG13 with the unrelated severe recessive HSPD1 infantile leukodystrophy.
Anchoring on the common SPG4 and not sequencing HSPD1 when initial testing is negative.
Missing a treatable acquired myelopathy by omitting imaging and metabolic screening before assigning a genetic label.
Overlooking a subtle dominant family history given the variable age at onset and slow progression.
references: Clinical neurology textbook — motor system and hereditary spastic paraplegias
management: No disease-specific therapy exists; reduce lower-limb spasticity with oral antispasticity agents such as baclofen or tizanidine, escalating to focal botulinum toxin injection for problematic adductor or gastrocnemius-soleus tone
Regular physiotherapy, muscle stretching and gait training with ankle-foot orthoses to preserve mobility and prevent contractures
Treat corticospinal bladder urgency with antimuscarinic agents alongside urological review
Consider intrathecal baclofen for severe spasticity refractory to oral and focal treatment
Surveillance of mobility, falls risk and contractures, with occupational therapy and timely provision of walking aids
Autosomal dominant inheritance warrants genetic counselling and cascade HSPD1 testing, distinguishing heterozygous SPG13 from the severe biallelic hypomyelinating leukodystrophy
Re-evaluate the diagnosis and refer to specialist neurology if prominent sensory, cerebellar or cognitive signs emerge, as these argue against SPG13
